newsitem.title: USA: API's focus on government intrusion, not Texaco.
newsitem.headline: API's focus on government intrusion, not Texaco.

text.p: - Oil executives gathered for the annual American Petroleum Institute (API) meeting adhered to the script, producing only an occasional public reference to the swirl of controversy engulfing Texaco Inc.

But calls by civil rights leaders on Tuesday for a national boycott of Texaco products until the company settles a pending discrimation suit filed by employees were a hot topic in private conversations.
On the podiums however, the issue of government and what industry should expect from a second Clinton administration were featured topics.

Still, racial diversity among the workforces employed by oil companies was in the spotlight at least once, when the head of Exxon Corp blamed education as the culprit for the low numbers of black and other minorities on payrolls.

Lee Raymond, Exxon's chief executive officer and the chairman of API's board, denied the oil industry works to keep minorities out, saying there are not enough qualified candidates for what is essentially a technical business.
"Our business is largely technical. We have to hire engineers to do that work," Raymond said at a press conference.
"If someone doesn't get on the right science or math track in the sixth or seventh grade, you can't become an engineer," Raymond noted.
"We can't hire what's not there," Raymond said, adding it takes "very long term" planning to get people in position to have the right training to take oil industry jobs.
"Until you start to grow with the right educational system, there won't be a fix for this problem," Raymond said.
Exxon noted it was one of the founding companies behind the formation of the United Negro College Fund. Raymond is a board member of that organization.
Many oil companies said they employ special programs to recruit black college graduates, and some specifically train employees to understand and practice "non-exclusionary" policies.
A spokesman for British Petroleum Co Plc said more than 1,000 middle managers have been trained in compulsory courses on working in a diverse environment.
He also said BP also sponsors minority engineering scholarship programs at three traditionally black schools: Tuskeegee Institute, Florida A&M and North Carolina A&T.
Still, the number of higher level, minority executives were not immediately known at BP.
One industry executive at the conference said just as the number of women in the oil business has grown in recent years, the number of black and other groups could as well.
"Look around, you see a lot more women in here, that wasn't true only a few years back," said the executive.
However, the number of blacks at the convention was miniscule. Just as many of the upper offices are barren of black executives, the overall industry lags.
Department of Labor statistics for the end of 1995 showed the number of workers employed in the oil and gas extraction sector for the entire nation at 337,000.

Of that number, 3.9 percent were black, 7.4 percent Hispanic and 16.2 percent women, with a statistician for the department saying nationally, blacks make up just over 10 percent of the workforce, women 46.1 percent and Hispanics nearly nine percent.
The data on women include all racial breakdowns.
